title: NP-hardness of improper learning of \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\)
formal: Is there an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(b\ge a\), there are an integer \(r\ge1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time oracle reduction \(R_b\) which decides SAT with success probability at least \(2/3\) using the following agnostic circuit-learning oracle? A query is a Boolean sampling circuit producing a distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\times\{0,1\}\). Every oracle reply must be a circuit \(h\) of size at most \((m+1)^{b}\) satisfying \[L_D(h)\le\min_{g\in\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}((m+1)^{a})}L_D(g)+(m+1)^{-r}.\] The reduction must succeed for every sequence of valid replies. The exponent \(r\), reduction and its running-time polynomial may depend on \(b\), but not on the SAT instance. No cryptographic or unproved complexity assumption is part of the target. This selects the source's agnostic, efficiently samplable-distribution reduction formulation.
why: This asks whether learning general small circuits remains hard when the learner is free to use a different and polynomially larger representation. Establishing such hardness from SAT would connect worst-case NP difficulty with a central general learning task, while the known links to witness encryption expose consequences beyond learning itself.
status_note: Open in the CCC 2025 source. The subsequent ECCC TR26-091 checked on 2026-09-14 establishes related conditional hardness under cryptographic and proof-complexity assumptions, not the unconditional claim here. The selected formal oracle-reduction variant and its quantifier order are explicit; this bounded check is not an exhaustive literature or proof verification.

progress.text: Goldberg and Kabanets relate restricted forms of learning hardness to witness encryption and explicitly leave general improper circuit-learning NP-hardness open.

Goldberg, Juvekar and Kabanets give randomized reduction results for full-support PAC learning under additional cryptographic and proof-complexity assumptions. The checked statement does not eliminate those assumptions.

category_assignment.reason: The question asks for NP-hardness of improper learning for polynomial-size circuits; witness encryption is the source context.

importance.reason: A major hardness question for unrestricted polynomial-size hypothesis representations, linking worst-case NP difficulty, agnostic learning and cryptographic assumptions; substantially broader than hardness of proper learning for one representation.

sentences: The question asks whether SAT reduces to agnostic learning of general polynomial-size Boolean circuits.
The learning oracle receives a circuit sampling labeled examples and returns an approximately optimal hypothesis.
The returned hypothesis may use an arbitrarily larger fixed polynomial size than the comparator circuits.
The reduction must work with every valid oracle reply and without additional cryptographic assumptions.
A June 2026 follow-up gives related conditional hardness, leaving the unconditional target unresolved.

definitions:
A Boolean circuit is an explicitly listed directed acyclic graph with named input wires, constant zero and one wires, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and named output wires. Its size is its number of noninput gates, including constant gates. Gate types and predecessor indices are encoded in binary in topological order; all input and output counts are explicit. Write \(\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}(s)\) for the binary functions on \(m\) input bits computed by one-output circuits with at most \(s\) gates. A language is in \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) if its restriction to each input length is computed by a circuit family with polynomial size; those circuits need not be generated uniformly.

A sampling-circuit query has some number \(q\ge0\) of random input bits and \(m+1\) output bits, with \(m\ge1\). Uniform independent bits in \(\{0,1\}^{q}\) induce the joint distribution \(D\); the first \(m\) outputs are the example and the last is its label. Labels may be noisy and need not be realizable by a small circuit. The risk is \(L_D(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\). The oracle returns the full description of a predictor satisfying the displayed excess-risk guarantee. An answer always exists because the smaller comparator family is finite, contains constant functions, and is included in the allowed output family. The oracle itself has no computational restriction. It may select different valid circuits based on the query history; the reduction must work for all such selections, not only for a favorable learning rule.

The reduction is a randomized multitape Turing machine using independent fair bits. For each fixed \(b\), one polynomial in the SAT input bit length bounds its running time on every random tape and response history, counting construction of all sampling circuits and reading all reply descriptions; oracle computation is uncharged. Queries may be adaptive and may have different \(m,q\). In particular, the entire sampling circuit and every reply must have polynomial encoding length in the reduction's input length. The reduction may inspect hypothesis descriptions and evaluate them; it has no additional oracle or advice. SAT uses an explicit syntax-tree encoding of AND, OR and NOT formulas, with malformed encodings rejected. Probability of a correct SAT answer is over the reduction's coins, for each fixed input and each valid response policy.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such an exponent \(a\) and reductions exist, or a proof of the negation. A positive answer must cover every polynomial output-size exponent \(b\ge a\), allowing the stated dependence of the reduction on \(b\). Hardness only when the predictor is restricted to the target size, or only under an additional cryptographic assumption, does not suffice. A negative answer must rule out the displayed family of reductions, not merely one restricted reduction technique.

context_blocks.text: An improper learner may return a larger circuit than any circuit in the comparator class. Showing hardness only for size-preserving output can therefore leave an efficient improper learner possible. The quantification over every fixed polynomial output-size bound makes this distinction explicit.

The source defines learning reductions by giving the oracle a sampling circuit for a distribution and receiving a sufficiently accurate hypothesis. This card retains that oracle interface. Sampling distributions are generated by the reduction; the task does not give a practical learner arbitrary target membership queries.

The polynomial target-size exponent is fixed before the allowed output exponent. For each allowed output exponent the reduction may be different. Adaptive randomized Turing reductions are allowed; the card does not impose the additional deterministic, nonadaptive, witness-mapping or honesty conditions used in some of the source’s cryptographic consequences.

The June 2026 paper proves conditional hardness for a related full-support learning problem. It assumes a strong indistinguishability obfuscator and a lower-bound hypothesis for propositional proof systems. These are substantive assumptions, so the result does not by itself give the unconditional reduction asked for here.
